region.en: Country estate and Seoul official's house (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 鄉莊與漢京官邸（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Anecdote published in The Korea Review, Vol. 5 No. 5 (May 1905), by Yi Chong-won

source.work: The Korea Review, Vol. 5 No. 5, May 1905, 'The Magic Ox-Cure' by Yi Chong-won, eBook #58243

summary.en: Mr. Cho, tiring of the otium cum dignitate of provincial life, spends ten years as an ante-room flatterer to a high Seoul dignitary until he is bankrupt; the official, receiving his gifts with complacency but offering no position, dismisses him with 'Of course you will consult your own convenience.' Overtaken by a storm on the road home, Cho shelters with an old woman whose farmer husband belabors the sleeping guest with four fairy sticks while she fastens a halter around his neck — Cho goes on four legs, lows like an ox, and is taken to market and sold to a bibulous butcher. Left tied while the butcher drinks, he crowds through the hedge, eats a turnip, and stands up again as two-legged Cho; he steals back the four sticks, taps the sleeping Seoul official lightly — two horns grow from his forehead and his hands turn to hoofs — then returns as the wonder-worker whose turnip powder, administered before the family, wipes out every evidence of the bestial metamorphosis. Honors pour in upon him, peysil unlimited and kwansey without alloy.
summary.zh: 趙某十年行賄於京官而無所得，破產還鄉。途中遇雨，投宿農家，夜被農夫以仙杖擊之，化為牛，繫於市，售與屠者。屠者飲酒，趙嚙田中蘿蔔而復人形。乃竊仙杖，潛擊京官，使其首生角、手成蹄。趙旋以蘿蔔粉為『秘藥』醫之，官復原形，趙由是顯貴。

sensitivity.note: Printed variant of the Old Timber Top tale-type (cf. korean-old-timber-top-bull); no living-community restriction.

passages.text: As he was on his way he was overtaken by a severe storm. At last he sighted a little cottage among the trees; the old woman relented and let him in. How long he had slept he could not tell, when he awoke with a start to the sound of a man's voice asking of the woman gruffly, 'What time is it, anyway? I must get off to market early with that ox'; whereupon the couple entered Cho's room, the man carrying four sticks and the wife a halter. The farmer dragged the bedclothes off the guest, bestrode his chest and began to belabor him with the sticks, while the woman fastened the halter around his neck. He was then dragged out of the room, but to his horror he found himself going on four legs, and when he tried to speak he could only low like an ox.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Yi Chong-won, 'The Magic Ox-Cure', Korea Review (May 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the market town he was herded with a drove of cattle, and at last a burly butcher came to terms with the farmer. When they came to a wine shop the ox was tied to a stake while the butcher indulged in the flowing bowl. Just over the hedge was a field of succulent turnips; Mr. Cho managed to get loose from the stake and, crowding through the hedge, pulled a turnip and began to munch it. After the first bite a curious sensation overtook him: a thrill went through him from tail to horns and in another instant he found himself an ox no longer but the same old two-legged Cho as of old.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Yi Chong-won, 'The Magic Ox-Cure', Korea Review (May 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Sticks and turnips! Sticks and turnips!' he repeated over and over again as if it were a magic formula. He found and secured the four sticks with which the work had been done, and made a silent and speedy departure toward Seoul. He found the official sleeping profoundly, knelt beside the recumbent form and, taking only two of the sticks, began tapping very gently upon the sleeper: soon two horns grew out of the sleeper's head and his two hands gradually turned into hoofs. Then Mr. Cho appeared upon the scene, announced that there was one remedy that had been left untried, purchased a turnip at the corner grocery, cut it up fine, macerated it and dried it into a powder, and administered the potent drug: an instant later the two horns receded into the cranium and the hoofs changed their form, and at last all evidence of the bestial metamorphosis was wiped out. Honors poured in upon him, peysil unlimited and kwansey without alloy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Yi Chong-won, 'The Magic Ox-Cure', Korea Review (May 1905); not verbatim.

texts.period: Koryo festival of 918 CE, described by Frederick Starr, Korean Buddhism (1918), citing Hulbert

source.work: Frederick Starr, Korean Buddhism: History—Condition—Art (1918), 'History', eBook #47957

summary.en: At his new capital Songdo, General Wang-on (Wang-gon, Taejo of Koryo), ending the first year of his rule in 918, held a famous festival: an enormous lantern hung about with hundreds of others under a tent made of a network of silken cords; music an important element; representations of dragons, birds, elephants, horses, carts and boats; dancing prominent, a hundred forms of entertainment — each official wearing the long flowing sleeves and carrying the ivory memorandum tablets, and the king watching from a high platform. When Wang-on died in 942 he left his son ten rules of conduct for his guidance as king, three of them religious: continue to recognize Buddhism as the state religion; build no more monasteries, too much money having already been expended upon them; and establish an annual Buddhist festival of the same nature as the one he had celebrated — the origin of the Yondung-hoe, the lantern festival that endures in Korean Buddhism.
summary.zh: 高麗太祖王建都松京，元年（918）舉大燃燈會：巨燈居中，千百盞環之，張絲網為棚；樂舞百戲，龍、象、車、舟之形畢陳；群臣廣袖持笏，王登高臺觀焉。王臨終遺訓十條，其三涉佛：一奉佛教為國教，二勿再建寺（費已巨），三歲行燃燈會如元年之制。朝鮮佛教燃燈之俗由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Historical festival record; the lantern festival (Yondung-hoe) remains living practice — described here as historical origin, not liturgy.

passages.text: At his new capital he ended the first year of his rule, 918, with a famous festival of which we have a description: there was an enormous lantern, hung about with hundreds of others under a tent made of a network of silken cords. Music was an important element. There were also representations of dragons, birds, elephants, horses, carts and boats. Dancing was prominent and there were in all a hundred forms of entertainment. Each official wore the long, flowing sleeves, and each carried the ivory memorandum tablets. The king sat on a high platform and watched the entertainment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Starr, Korean Buddhism (1918), citing Hulbert; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Wang-on died in 942, he left a written message for his son and successor: it contained ten rules of conduct for his guidance as king. Three had to do with religion. In the first rule he advised his son to continue to recognize Buddhism as the state religion; the second rule was that he should build no more monasteries, too much money having already been expended upon them; the sixth of the rules was for the establishment of an annual Buddhist festival of the same nature as the one he had celebrated at the end of his first year.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Starr, Korean Buddhism (1918), citing Hulbert; not verbatim.

title.en: Ichadon's Blood Ran White as Milk

region.zh: 新羅刑場（慶州）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Martyrdom of AD 527 (Hulbert dates the execution 524); chronicled in Samguk Sagi and Samguk Yusa, here from Hulbert's History of Korea (1905)

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 10, eBook #52127

summary.en: The high priest Ichadon (Yi Cha-don) offers his own life to legalize Buddhism in Silla, promising that his blood will flow white as milk — and it does, converting the court overnight.
summary.zh: 高僧異次頓以身殉法，預言其血白如乳，果然，新羅舉國皈佛。

sensitivity.note: Buddhist martyr miracle; no living-community restriction on academic retelling.

narrative.en: In the early sixth century the kingdom of Silla wavered over the new religion from the west. King Beopheung had come so completely under the influence of the monks that the old aristocracy feared their power would soon swallow the ancient offices of state; the courtiers used every means to induce the king to moderate his views, and at last won from him a reluctant assent to the execution of the high priest, Ichadon (Yi Cha-don). Tradition says that Ichadon had himself foreseen the bargain and chosen it: brought to the place of execution, he exclaimed that when they slew him his blood would flow not red like blood but white as milk, and then they would know that Buddhism was true. When the head was severed from the trunk, his blood flowed white like milk. None could gainsay the evidence, and from that day Buddhism advanced with rapid steps in Silla; the following year the king made a law against the killing of animals, and the temple at Heungnyun-sa rose on the site of the old sacred grove. The episode is Korea's founding martyrdom — a miracle of proof modeled on the lot-flower and white-blood wonders of the wider Buddhist world, and retold in the Samguk Sagi annals and, with richer legendary detail, in the Samguk Yusa's Feats of the Monk Ichadon. In the Yusa version, Ichadon had proposed the stratagem himself to the king: if they kill me and my blood turns white, then Your Majesty may build the temples without fear — and after his death his face showed no change, and a great dragon and a shower of flowers attended his burial on Mt. Cheonseong. The officials who had opposed the faith read the sign and confessed; the king proclaimed that no man should henceforth hinder the law of the Buddha, and the ten temple compounds of the royal foundation rose in the capital. Later generations of Korean monks kept the feast of the martyr, and his shrine became one of the stations of the Silla Buddhist year. Whether read as history, hagiography, or politics dressed as portent, the story fixes the moment when the sacred kingship of Silla and the Dharma made their pact: the martyr's white blood purchased, once and for all, the freedom of the sangha in Korea, and the boundary between the old blood-sacrifice of the aristocracy and the new compassion-ethic of the monasteries was drawn in a color no one could deny.

functions: Sanctions the legal adoption of Buddhism in Silla as a miracle of proof witnessed by the court
Provides the martyr-model for later Korean Buddhist hagiography and temple origin stories
Legitimates royal patronage of the sangha against aristocratic resistance

title.en: Sim Chung's Leap: Daughter of the Star Who Bought Her Father's Eyes

region.en: Indangsu strait; Dragon King's palace; Seoul palace (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 印塘海與龍宮（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Pansori tale cycle; Allen's English rendering (1889) of the 18th-19th c. Namwon tradition

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 8 'Sim Chung', eBook #55539

summary.en: Blind Sim Hyun is promised restored sight for three hundred bags of rice; his daughter Sim Chung sells herself to the sea merchants as the sacrifice that calms the evil spirit of Indangsu, is received into the Dragon King's palace as a banished star, returns in a flower, becomes queen of Korea, and at a feast of all the blind men of the realm tears the scales from her father's eyes.
summary.zh: 沈清賣身祭海，龍宮納為星宿之女，借花還陽，冊為王后，大宴天下盲者，其父拭目而明。

sensitivity.note: Filial-sacrifice motif; human-sacrifice element handled at summary level; no living-community restriction.

narrative.en: The Pansori of the Song of Chunhyang's contemporary, the Song of Sim Cheong, opens in the household of the blind gentleman Sim Hyun, whose beautiful and accomplished wife has waited fifteen childless years before dreaming that a star comes down to her from the skies. The daughter born of that dream, Sim Chung, has cheeks like full-blown roses and wisdom beyond her years; when the mother dies the father emerges from grief totally blind, and in ten years the homestead is spent. Wandering in his darkness, the blind man falls into a ditch and is found by the old priest of the mountain-fortress temple, who prophesies: make an offering of three hundred bags of rice to the Buddha of the temple, and you will be restored to sight, given rank and dignity, while your daughter becomes the first woman in all Korea. He signs the order he cannot pay, and pounds rice in stone mortars while his daughter begs and tends him. Hearing that the sea merchants who sail yearly to China will buy a maiden to throw into Indangsu, the strait where an evil spirit wrecks their boats, Sim Chung decides the dream is fulfilled: she puts on old clothes, fasts that she may look haggard, and tells her father she is going to bow at her mother's grave. The merchant's overseer is struck by her dignity — 'I did not know that such filial piety existed outside the works of the ancients' — and the rice is paid. On the appointed morning, dressed in bridal garments at the head of a procession of boats, Sim Chung prays to heaven, bids them goodbye, and leaps into the sea; above, the waves subside and the sea becomes like a lake. Below, she wakes in a little boat drawn by fishes, is borne to the palace of the Sea King through forests of waving plants and walks of polished black marble, and learns her own past from the Dragon King: she was once a star, banished to earth for abuse of her office as cup-bearer to the King of Heaven, sent as daughter to the man who had been her lover. Heaven, seeing her filial piety, repents. When the time comes to return, a great flower is brought into her chamber; hidden inside it she floats to the surface, is netted by her friend the merchant, and presented to the King, who keeps the perfumed plant in a glass house. Discovered walking in the moonlight — the flower vanishing and leaving her standing alone — she is revealed as the brilliant star that astronomers saw descend upon the palace; the widowed king makes her his queen in the royal wedding hall. Lonely for her father, she asks that all the blind men of the country be summoned to a feast of clothing, food and cash, and watches three days from her pavilion; on the third evening a feeble old man in rags comes tottering up, and the Queen screams 'My father! my father!' and falls senseless at his feet. 'Away with these sightless orbs!' — the old man tears at his eyes with his nails, the scales fall away, and he stands rejoicing in his sight; the king gives him rank, a house, and a bride, fulfilling the last of the prophecy of both the aged priest and the King of the Sea. The tale is performed today on both the wanpan and the dongpyeonje oral lines of the pansori Simcheong-ga, and its indangsu leap remains the emblem of Korean filial devotion.

functions: Commemorates Korean filial piety (hyo) as the supreme virtue, retold in every school anthology
Sanctions the historical use of sea sacrifice and its abolition narratives
Provides the queenly-return model for female destiny in Korean tale tradition

passages.text: In case you make an offering of three hundred bags of rice to the Buddha of our temple, you will be restored to sight, you will be given rank and dignity, while your daughter will become the first woman in all Korea. Sim Chung, hearing that the sea merchants would buy a maiden to quiet the evil spirit of the Indangsu, decided that it must be the fulfilment of her dream: she put on old clothes and fasted while journeying, that she might look wan and haggard, like one in mourning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: She was dressed in bridal garments furnished by the merchant; Sim Chung prayed to heaven, bade them all good-by, and leaped into the sea. Above, all was quiet, the waves subsided, the sea became like a lake, and the boats passed on their way unmolested. When she regained her consciousness she was seated in a little boat drawn by fishes, and pretty maidens were giving her to drink from a carved jade bottle: we are servants of the King of the Sea, and we are taking you to his palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Queen scrutinized the feeble old man in rags, she screamed, My father! my father! and fell at his feet senseless. He tore at his eyes with his nails, and to his utter amazement and joy the scales fell away, and he stood rejoicing in his sight once more. His Majesty made the old man an officer of high rank, thereby fulfilling the last of the prophecy of both the aged priest and the King of the Sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Chun Yang, the Faithful Dancing-Girl Wife

region.en: Kwang-han Pavilion, Namwon; magistrate's yamen and prison (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 廣寒樓與南原官署（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Pansori tale cycle of the Namwon tradition; Allen's English rendering (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 7 'Chun Yang', eBook #55539

summary.en: The scholar's son Toh Ryung and the kisaeng's daughter Chun Yang pledge themselves in writing for a hundred years at Kwang-han Pavilion; when a corrupt new magistrate tries to force her, she chooses prison, the cangue and the threat of death over dishonor — and is freed when Toh Ryung, returned as the King's disguised inspector, reveals his seal at the magistrate's birthday feast.
summary.zh: 夢龍與春香廣寒樓定情，立百年之券。新使君脅之，春香寧死不屈，荷枷入獄。夢龍以暗察使微服還鄉，於壽宴出御印，救其妻，誅貪吏。

sensitivity.note: Pansori classic; magistrate coercion summarized; no living-community restriction.

narrative.en: At the rarest of views, the Kwang-han Pavilion in Namwon, where the spirits themselves are said to frequent the place for its beauty, the sixteen-year-old Toh Ryung, son of the Prefect, watches a vision shoot into the air: a girl on a garden swing, her shoeless feet among the peach blossoms, her hairpin snapping on a rock. She is Chun Yang Ye, Fragrant Spring, born at midnight of the eighth day of the fourth moon, the lantern festival, an hour after his own birth — 'Heaven must have intended us to be man and wife.' She is no foolish thing: a gee sang by name but an honorable woman by choice, she will not be taken without a writing; and Toh Ryung, scaling the wall at night while his father sleeps, signs the memorandum — 'Meeting for the first time, I pledge myself for one hundred years; to be her faithful husband. Should I change, show this paper to the magistrate.' They drink the elixir of youth over the wine, and pledge that when death comes she will enter a flower and he a butterfly, resting on her bosom. When the father is raised to Secretary of Finance, they part with a crystal mirror and a jade ring; in Namwon a new magistrate arrives, a hard-faced politician resolved to marry the matchless beauty, and when Chun Yang answers 'A thousand deaths first' she is chained and thrown into prison, and at last wears the huge neck-encircling board of the condemned. Her gift-mirror breaks in her dream; the blind fortune-teller reads the sticks and answers that her husband has passed his examinations, been promoted, and will soon come to her. In Seoul, Toh Ryung wins the grand guaga and asks for the arduous duties of Ussa, the King's disguised inspector; as a beggar in straw sandals he hears the farmers curse the Prefect whose heart is 'as hard and unbending as the dead heart of the ancient oak.' At the magistrate's birthday feast — wine to flow like water, dancing girls from the whole district — the beggar forces his way in, demands a wine-song of his own, and then writes on the wall: 'The oil that enriches the food of the official is but the life blood of the down-trodden people, whose tears are of no more merit in the eyes of the oppressor than the drippings of a burning candle.' At the height of the uproar he takes out the King's seal: terror blanches the half-drunken faces, the host is caught crawling under his own house and bound in chains, and Chun Yang, carried in shackled to answer charges, hears his own voice and faints in his arms. The mother dashes away her dishes and tears around for joy — 'What a delightful birthday surprise for a cruel magistrate!' The marriage is solemnized publicly at Seoul, the Ussa is raised to a high and just office, and the country rings with the praises of his faithful wife, who became the mother of many children. The pansori Chunhyang-ga, performed today on both the wanpan and dongpyeonje lines, is Korea's national love-epic, sung each year at the Chunhyang Festival in Namwon around the garden where the swing once flew.

passages.text: Instantly the young man took up paper and brush, and wrote: A memorandum. Desiring to enjoy the spring scenery, I came to Kang Hal Loo. There I saw for the first time my heaven-sent bride. Meeting for the first time, I pledge myself for one hundred years; to be her faithful husband. Should I change, show this paper to the magistrate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Never, she bravely cried. A thousand deaths first. The man was fairly beside himself with wrath, and ordered her chained and thrown into prison at once; she passed the night in bowing before Heaven and calling on the gods and her husband to release her, while her mother scolded her for clinging to a faithless husband and the neighbors assured her she had done just right and would yet be rewarded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: To the surprise of all, the beggar claimed that as the other guests each had a fair gee sang to sing a wine song while they drank, he should be treated likewise; and in return for his food and wine he wrote: The oil that enriches the food of the official is but the life blood of the down-trodden people. The Ussa took out his official seal; at sight of the King's seal terror blanched the faces of the half-drunken men, the wicked host was caught crawling under the house and bound with chains, and Chun Yang, borne in shackles to answer charges, heard his own voice and fainted in his arms.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Tal-geui the Nine-Tailed Fox: The Kumiho's First Portrait

region.en: Mountain cave above the Shang court (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Fox-concubine legend transmitted through Chinese Shang-dynasty lore and Korean annalistic tradition; Hulbert's English telling (1905)

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 2, eBook #52127

summary.en: The beautiful concubine Tal-geui enslaves with a smile; the statesman Pi-gan traces her to a mountain cave where foxes fawn on her, kills her kin and robs their white breast-fur, and dies at her demand — but at the knife he curses her back into her true shape, a white fox with nine tails, which leaps from the window and escapes.
summary.zh: 妲己媚主，殺害忠良。比干偵知其為狐，盡誅其族，剝其白裘以進。妲己知族滅，求剖比干之心。比干臨刑喝其現形，遂化九尾白狐，破窗而遁。

sensitivity.note: The kumiho (nine-tailed fox) motif is central to Korean folklore; this is the Sino-Korean ur-variant (Daji); no living-community restriction.

narrative.en: Korean folklore's most feared shape-shifter, the kumiho or nine-tailed fox-woman, has its ur-portrait in the annalistic legend of Tal-geui, the concubine of the last Shang emperor. Wonderful in her beauty, she is surpassing so when she smiles: whoever she smiles upon is fascinated as by a serpent, and forced to comply with whatever request she makes. Pondering on this, the statesman Pi-gan decides that she must be a fox in human shape, for it is well known that if an animal tastes of water that has lain twenty years in a human skull it acquires the power to assume human shape at will. He sets inquiries on foot, and discovers that she makes a monthly visit to a certain mountain, ascending alone and leaving her train of attendants at the foot. Armed detectives follow her unseen and watch her enter a cave near the summit, from which she emerges accompanied by a pack of foxes who leap about her and fawn upon her in evident delight. When she leaves, the spies enter, put the foxes to the sword, and cut from each body the piece of white fur always found on the breast of the fox. When Tal-geui next meets the emperor, dressed in a sumptuous white fur robe, she shudders but does not yet guess the truth; a month later, entering the cave, she beholds the festering remains of her kindred. On her way home she plans her revenge, and adorning herself in all her finery she enters the imperial presence and exerts her fascination to the utmost. 'I hear,' she says at last, 'that there are seven orifices in the heart of every good man. I fain would put it to the test. I would that I might see the heart of Pi-gan.' His soul revolts from the act, yet he has no power to refuse; and as the executioner's knife is plunged into the victim's breast, Pi-gan cries that she is no woman but a fox in disguise, and charges her to resume her natural shape. Instantly hair springs forth upon her face, her nails grow long, and bursting from her garments she stands revealed — a white fox with nine tails. With one parting snarl at the assembled court she leaps from the window and makes good her escape. The story is, in effect, the Chou-dynasty fall of Shang as moralized by Korean historiography, and it fixes the grammar of the kumiho tale: a woman too beautiful, a smile that binds, a beast that gained its shape from drinking skull-water, the white breast-fur as tell, and the heart of the righteous man demanded as proof of virtue. In later Korean tellings the fox sheds her tails one by one as she approaches the human, eats liver, wears the shape of a bride or a schoolgirl, and is unmasked by dogs, mirrors or her own tail showing beneath the skirt; Im Bang's seventeenth-century collections record fox-women at the Hill Pagoda and wild-cat doubles at the chestnut table, and the motif remains a fixture of modern film and drama. Read as myth-history, Tal-geui's legend teaches the same boundary lesson as her sisters in every land: the beautiful stranger may be the beast, and the wise man's own death may be the price of proving it.

functions: Explains the origin and detection-signs of the kumiho (fox-woman) figure
Frames political downfall through the moralized figure of the dangerous female stranger
Marks the boundary between human and animal shape-shifting in Korean lore

variants.name: Daji of the Shang (Fengshen Yanyi tradition)
variants.text_tradition: Chinese novel Investiture of the Gods (16th c.) and earlier chronicle notices
variants.summary: The same fox-concubine Daji destroys the Shang; the Korean telling folds her into the origins of the kumiho.

variants.summary: A fox-woman visits a scholar at midnight and is caught and bitten on his back.

passages.text: The concubine Tal-geui was wonderfully beautiful, but surpassingly so when she smiled: at such times the person upon whom she smiled was fascinated as by a serpent and forced to comply with whatever request she made. Pondering this, Pi-gan decided that she must be a fox in human shape, for it is well known that if an animal tastes of water that has lain twenty years in a human skull it acquires the power to assume human shape at will.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 2 (1905); not verbatim.
